source.public_versification_note: Public and Hebrew verse numbering align throughout Genesis 46–50.

key_decisions.decision: Renders the future idiom without imposing an end-of-world scheme and retains Jacob’s claim to speak about what will befall them.
Retains the water image, loss of precedence, bed violation, and abrupt second-to-third-person shift rather than smoothing away the outburst.
Preserves their solidarity in violence; chooses the traditional swords sense of the uncertain final noun and identifies that uncertainty in a note.
Preserves Jacob’s refusal of association, honor parallelism, human killing, and deliberate animal harm; collective singulars are rendered naturally as plural.
Keeps the curse directed at anger/fury, the first-person scattering, and the parallel national names without adding later tribal outcomes.
Retains praise/name wordplay in apparatus, the concrete domination image, and the broader father’s-sons formulation.
Preserves cub-to-adult imagery, the second/third-person alternation, prey, and the rhetorical question; does not insert an acquittal over Joseph’s sale.
Retains the opaque pinned Shiloh reading in the text, the two rule symbols, and peoples; notes rival construals without making one disputed messianic identification the translation.
Keeps the extravagant concrete vine/donkey and wine/garment images, including blood of grapes; no prose explanation replaces the poetry.
Chooses causal with for the two min phrases while noting comparative alternatives; does not treat the verse as a literal physiological prediction.
Preserves coast, ships, and Sidon without altering the poem to fit a later territorial map.
Retains the animal and bone-strength image; selects saddlebags for the disputed resting-place term with sheepfolds noted.
Preserves the movement from attractive rest and land to burden and coerced labor without turning it into cheerful service.
Carries the repeated raid root and rear/heel image, with the Gad wordplay noted rather than replaced with unrelated military language.
Follows the pinned doe and sayings vocalization despite the mixed imagery; notes the alternative fawns reading rather than silently changing the source.
Preserves the repeated fruitful phrase and spring/wall image in the traditional botanical reading; notes the competing wild-donkey interpretation of the difficult Hebrew.
Preserves bow/arms and the hand image, retaining Stone rather than silently substituting Rock; makes the compressed divine-title syntax readable and notes its difficulty.
Retains the second-person shift and all three blessing realms, including female bodily imagery; treats divine clauses as continuing the prior source of strength without adding a new speaker.
Follows the pinned forebears construal rather than silently adopting ancient mountains; preserves hills, head/brow parallelism, and the ambiguous set-apart status in a note.
Retains the narrator’s blessing designation even for the harsh sayings and the exact twelve-tribe total.
Keeps gathered-to-people distinct from burial and lets the location continue into the following verse without inventing an afterlife explanation.
Preserves the physical last movement and gathered-to-people formula without reducing the verse to a bare death notice.
